clue.text: Actor, get inside!" order?

parts.note: an instruction in a script telling a performer to go into the set is the kind of order meant

explanation.surface: Someone barks at an actor to come indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Directions printed in a play script tell performers where to move, such as entering or leaving.

clue.text: A throne overthrown for a second

indicators.note: a toppled throne is thrown about, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A monarch's seat is toppled in an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a second' means one more of the same, not a moment of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for a second helping is asking for one more.

clue.text: Nothing odd in flat

explanation.surface: Nothing strange about a level apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A number with nothing odd about it is divisible by two, and a flat surface is level and smooth.

clue.text: How batsman is seen as an example…

explanation.surface: A cricket batsman's position is offered as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, IN STANCE: a batsman at the crease is 'in' and stands in his stance. In cricket the batsman is the player hitting the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A case in point, cited to illustrate a general claim.

clue.text: … lure England's openers to catch

parts.note: the opening two letters of the word England
to catch an animal is to trap it

explanation.surface: Tempting England's opening batsmen into being caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'openers' here takes the first two letters of 'England', not just one; the cricket picture (openers, catch) is a cover story.
explanation.definitionFit: To lure someone into a snare is to trick them into a trap.

clue.text: Possibly hate to stop this cosmetic?.

indicators.note: signals that the letters of the following words could be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A grooming product one might hate to give up.
explanation.definitionFit: A paste used to clean and whiten teeth, treated by the setter as a cosmetic.

clue.text: Supreme wear for boiler men?

explanation.surface: The finest clothing for men who stoke boilers.
explanation.definitionFit: The overall winner is supreme above all others, and a boilersuit-style protective garment is worn by workmen.

clue.text: Daily pressure that keeps office work down

parts.note: a daily is a newspaper published every day
weight is pressure bearing down

explanation.surface: The stress of the daily grind keeps office work down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps office work down' reads as stifling labour, but it means holding loose sheets in place on a desk.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy object placed on documents stops them blowing away.

clue.text: County house that held British records?

explanation.surface: A county mansion where British archives were stored.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerset is a county in south-west England, and Somerset House in London long held the register of births, marriages and deaths.
explanation.definitionFit: A shire of south-west England, and the London building that housed the national registry of births and deaths.

clue.text: Work sometime on musical drama

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a numbered work of music
an era is some period of time

explanation.surface: Working at some point on a stage musical.
explanation.definitionFit: A staged dramatic work set to music and sung throughout.

clue.text: Knave after a biscuit — there's a fine thing!

indicators.note: the knave's word is placed after the biscuit's word

parts.note: a cracker is a thin crisp biscuit
the knave in a pack of cards is the jack

explanation.surface: A rogue grabs a biscuit and exclaims at how good it is.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of admiration for something excellent, an old slang term of praise.

clue.text: Hindi demon in Maharashtra hubbub

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run formed by the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A demon makes a racket in an Indian state.
explanation.walkthrough: Maharashtra is a state of western India; the demon of Hindu myth said to swallow the sun at eclipses runs across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hindu mythology a serpent-like spirit that causes eclipses by swallowing the sun or moon.

clue.text: A RA, perhaps, to express in new way

annotationWithheld.why: A RA, perhaps, to express in new way: 'to express in new way' defines PARAPHRASE, but no reading of 'A RA, perhaps' supplies P-A-R-A-PHRASE; a letter or word looks lost in OCR and no scan is held
annotationWithheld.clue: A RA, perhaps, to express in new way

clue.text: But it is not like a bath-bun

definitions.text: But it is not like a bath-bun

parts.words: But it is not like a bath-bun
parts.note: a soft spongy item from the bath versus a baker's bun: one sort of cake is named after the bath item

explanation.surface: A remark comparing something to a currant bun from Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath bun is a sweet sugared bun from the city of Bath; the clue plays on a bath sponge, which is unlike it, and a cake that is.
explanation.definitionFit: A light airy cake whose texture resembles the absorbent bath item.

clue.text: Vehicle going fast is a hardtop

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
apace means swiftly

explanation.surface: A speeding vehicle is a car with a fixed roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hardtop' looks like a car body, matching the surface, but it means a hard shell on top of an animal's back.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard upper shell of a tortoise or crab, a natural rigid covering.

clue.text: Shout with' cry of pain not covered with feathers

parts.note: to shout is to call
ow is what one exclaims when hurt

explanation.surface: A yell and a yelp from a bird without plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: The original meaning, from Old English, was unfledged or bald; it now usually means immature.

clue.text: Solitaire for one besotted with Bunthorne

explanation.surface: A card game for a lovesick admirer of an aesthetic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunthorne is the poet in Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta, whose dairymaid heroine gives the work its title.
explanation.definitionFit: A card game played alone, and the milkmaid heroine of the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.

clue.text: Formerly, nurse to stretch out

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
to nurse a patient is to tend them

explanation.surface: A former nurse lengthens her reach.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen or reach further.

clue.text: Concerned with touching one among straying cattle

indicators.note: one piece goes in the middle of the other's letters
animals that stray wander out of their places, so the letters move around

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Stroking one beast in a wandering herd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straying' scrambles CATTLE into TACTLE, and 'among' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the sense of touch.

clue.text: Smoked beef? Done with butter, I go with that!

parts.note: something past is over and finished
a ram is an animal that butts with its head

explanation.surface: Someone happily agrees to a beef dish cooked in butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but a thing that butts: a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Seasoned and smoked cured meat, usually from the brisket of a cow.

clue.text: Regal as Elgar — or as large, perhaps?

definitions.text: Regal as Elgar — or as large, perhaps?

parts.words: Regal as Elgar — or as large, perhaps
parts.note: the clue lists words made by shuffling the same five letters, naming the device that links them

explanation.surface: Asking whether the composer Elgar was majestic or just big.
explanation.walkthrough: REGAL, ELGAR and LARGE use the same letters; the clue asks for the term for each of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A word formed by rearranging the letters of another.

clue.text: Spasmodic trouble for air ways

parts.note: airways reads as aviation routes but means the passages of the lungs, which spasm in this illness

explanation.surface: Fitful disruption to an airline's routes.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronic condition in which the bronchial tubes tighten in spasms, making breathing hard.

clue.text: Riding-post?

parts.note: a post read as a job or position held by someone who rides racehorses

explanation.surface: A post for tying horses.
explanation.definitionFit: The position or skill of a professional horse-race rider.

clue.text: The laundry-bay

explanation.surface: A laundry beside the bay.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wash is a large square bay on England's east coast between Lincolnshire and Norfolk.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes to be cleaned are the week's washing, and the bay on the east coast of England bears the same name.

clue.text: Partly patriotic, King Cole's fiddlers?

indicators.note: only a part of the following word is used, a run from its middle

explanation.surface: A loyal old monarch with his musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Old King Cole called for his fiddlers three.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme's king summoned three fiddlers, a group of three musicians.

clue.text: Initially, carbine held in normal attitude is for firing

indicators.note: the first letters of each of the next five words are taken

explanation.surface: A rifle held correctly ready for shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firing' looks like a gun going off, but it is what a kiln does to porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Porcelain is shaped and then baked in a kiln, so it is made for firing.

clue.text: Hooray! RN ordered to be unpaid

indicators.note: the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cheers as the Royal Navy is told to work for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the Royal Navy, which makes 'ordered' look like a naval command.
explanation.definitionFit: An honorary post is held without salary.

clue.text: Fellow's septemfid term, according to Jaques?

definitions.text: Fellow's septemfid term, according to Jaques?

parts.words: Fellow's septemfid term, according to Jaques
parts.note: septemfid means split into seven parts: a man's life span divided sevenfold, as a melancholy character in As You Like It describes it

explanation.surface: A scholarly question about a seven-part period of a man's life.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques is the courtier in Shakespeare's As You Like It whose 'All the world's a stage' speech divides life into seven stages.
explanation.definitionFit: The speech traces a life through seven stages, from infant to second childhood.
